name: AWS Mission Resilience Lens (MRL)
description: The AWS Mission Resilience Lens (MRL) is a targeted evaluation framework for highly regulated workloads. This lens includes best practices based on our experience reviewing these architectures, and includes additional content from both the AWS Operational Readiness Review program and the AWS Well-Architected Framework's Reliability pillar. AWS recommends supplementing this work with a full Well-Architected review when time permits. Reviews should be conducted at least annually or after significant architectural changes.

questions.title: What level of AWS Support do you have for your workload? Do you have support plans for your other dependencies?
questions.description: A well-defined and documented support plan is crucial for maintaining business continuity and minimizing downtime. It ensures clear procedures for handling incidents, managing service disruptions, and engaging with both internal teams and third-party vendors. Without proper documentation, organizations risk delayed response times, unclear escalation paths, and potential service level agreement (SLA) breaches.

choices.title: AWS Enterprise Support

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider upgrading to Enterprise Support for mission-critical workloads to benefit from faster response times and dedicated support.

helpfulResource.displayText: AWS Enterprise Support

choices.title: AWS Business Support

improvementPlan.displayText: If not using Business or Enterprise Support, upgrade to at least Business Support for production workloads to ensure adequate coverage.

helpfulResource.displayText: AWS Business Support

choices.title: AWS Developer Support

improvementPlan.displayText: Ensure you're not using Developer Support for production workloads, as it doesn't provide adequate coverage for mission-critical systems.

helpfulResource.displayText: AWS Developer Support

choices.title: Other dependencies (non-AWS) have no support plans

improvementPlan.displayText: Verify that all dependencies have appropriate support agreements in place. Having dependencies without support creates significant mission risk.

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if your non-AWS dependencies (such as operating systems, third-party applications, hardware, or services) do not have any formal support agreements or maintenance contracts in place.

choices.title: Other dependencies (non-AWS) are partially covered by support plans

improvementPlan.displayText: Review all dependencies to ensure they have full support coverage. Partial coverage may leave critical components without adequate support.

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if some, but not all, of your non-AWS dependencies have support agreements. This might include having support for major systems while smaller components lack coverage, or having different levels of support across different dependencies.

choices.title: Other dependencies (non-AWS) are fully covered by support plans

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement comprehensive support coverage for all dependencies to ensure consistent support across your entire solution.

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if all of your non-AWS dependencies have appropriate support agreements in place, with documented SLAs and clear escalation paths for each component critical to your mission.

choices.title: I don't know.

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this option if you are not aware of your current support status.

questions.title: Have you completed a Well-Architected Framework Review (WAFR) and addressed identified risks?
questions.description: A comprehensive Well-Architected Review includes six pillars. This lens focuses on mission resilience for highly regulated workloads. AWS recommends supplementing this work with a full Well-Architected review when time permits. Reviews should be conducted at least annually or after significant architectural changes.

choices.title: A Well-Architected Framework Review has been completed within the last 12 months

improvementPlan.displayText: Complete a Well-Architected Framework Review. Contact your AWS Account team for assistance.

helpfulResource.displayText: AWS Well-Architected Framework

choices.title: All high-risk findings from the WAFR have been resolved

improvementPlan.displayText: Address all high-risk findings identified in your WAFR. High-risk items represent significant mission risk.

helpfulResource.displayText: High-risk findings require immediate attention as they represent significant threats to workload resilience. Resolving these findings demonstrates a strong commitment to maintaining operational readiness.

choices.title: All medium-risk findings from the WAFR have been resolved

improvementPlan.displayText: Address remaining medium-risk findings identified in your WAFR to improve your architecture's resilience.

helpfulResource.displayText: Medium-risk findings, while less urgent than high-risk, still represent important opportunities to improve workload resilience and should be addressed in a timely manner.

choices.title: Regular WAFR reviews are scheduled and documented

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish and document a regular review schedule aligned with mission requirements and architectural changes.

helpfulResource.displayText: AWS Well-Architected Reviews Best Practices

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if no WAFR activities have been completed

questions.title: Is each component of your workload deployed to multiple locations?
questions.description: Locations can include AWS regions, availability zones (AZ), or on-premises datacenters. Consider mission requirements for high availability, recovery time objectives, and geographic separation when evaluating your deployment strategy.

choices.title: Multiple AWS regions

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider implementing multi-region deployment to enhance mission resilience. Multi-region architectures provide the highest level of availability and support disaster recovery requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: Multi-region deployment supports missions requiring specific recovery time objectives and enhanced resilience against regional failures.

choices.title: Single region (multiple AZs)

improvementPlan.displayText: If multi-region is not feasible, implement multi-AZ deployment as a minimum to protect against AZ failures. Deploy across at least two AZs with automated failover capabilities.

helpfulResource.displayText: Multi-AZ deployment pattern provides automated failover and balanced workload distribution across zones within a region.

choices.title: Single region (single AZ) and one or more on-premises location(s)

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice avoiding single AZ with on-premises hybrid deployment. Continue to avoid this pattern as it introduces unnecessary complexity and single points of failure.

helpfulResource.displayText: Hybrid architectures should leverage multiple AZs within AWS while maintaining robust connectivity to on-premises resources.

choices.title: Single region (single AZ only)

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice avoiding single-AZ deployment. Continue to avoid single-AZ architectures as they present significant availability risks and single points of failure.

helpfulResource.displayText: Single-AZ deployments lack resilience against zone failures. Review multi-AZ patterns for improved availability.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above deployment patterns match your workload's current architecture

questions.title: How do you back up data?
questions.description: Back up data, applications, and configuration to meet your requirements for recovery time objectives (RTO) and recovery point objectives (RPO). Understanding the methods, test frequency, assigned personnel, and the contract transition plan supports confidence in backups and recovery. (Aligns with AWS Well Architected Framework question Reliability #9)

choices.title: Identify and back up all data that needs to be backed up, or reproduce the data from sources

improvementPlan.displayText: Document and implement backup strategies for all critical data, leveraging native AWS service backup capabilities where possible.

helpfulResource.displayText: Understand and use the backup capabilities of the data services and resources used by the workload. Most services provide capabilities to back up workload data.

choices.title: Secure and encrypt backups

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement encryption and access controls for all backup data to ensure confidentiality and integrity.

helpfulResource.displayText: Control and detect access to backups using authentication and authorization. Prevent and detect if data integrity of backups is compromised using encryption.

choices.title: Perform data backup automatically

improvementPlan.displayText: Configure automated backup schedules based on RPO requirements and data criticality.

helpfulResource.displayText: Configure backups to be taken automatically based on a periodic schedule informed by the Recovery Point Objective (RPO), or by changes in the dataset. Critical datasets with low data loss requirements need to be backed up automatically on a frequent basis, whereas less critical data where some loss is acceptable can be backed up less frequently.

choices.title: Perform periodic recovery of the data to verify backup integrity and processes

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement regular backup recovery testing to validate RTO and RPO requirements are met.

helpfulResource.displayText: Validate that your backup process implementation meets your Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO) by performing a recovery test.

choices.title: Identify who is responsible for performing backups and periodically testing recovery

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish and document clear roles and responsibilities for backup operations and testing procedures.

helpfulResource.displayText: Clear ownership and responsibilities for backup operations and testing ensures consistent execution and accountability for data recovery capabilities.

choices.title: Transition plan in-place for contract turnover

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and maintain documentation for backup procedures and create transition plans for personnel or contract changes.

helpfulResource.displayText: A documented transition plan ensures backup and recovery processes continue uninterrupted during contract changes or personnel transitions.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these best practices.

questions.title: Have SLAs/SLOs or other availability goals been determined for your workload?
questions.description: Service Level Objectives (SLOs) are defined targets that organizations set for themselves to ensure that their services meet certain performance standards. Service Level Agreements (SLAs) are formal agreements that outline the service provider's responsibilities and the consequences of not meeting them.

choices.title: Service Level Agreements (SLAs) have been defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Define and document SLAs that specify availability targets and maximum allowable disruption periods. Common targets range from 99% to 99.999% availability.

helpfulResource.displayText: Architect your product to meet availability targets and uptime service level agreements (SLAs). Verify that your architecture and operational processes support your committed SLAs.

choices.title: Service Level Objectives (SLOs) have been defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Define and document SLOs for all services, including those used internally. SLOs should clearly communicate expected performance and availability standards.

helpfulResource.displayText: SLOs have been established for all services, whether customer-facing or internal, to ensure performance standards are met and support KPI measurements.

choices.title: Service Level Agreements (SLAs) have not been defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice having defined SLAs. Continue maintaining clear SLA definitions as they are crucial for setting expectations and ensuring service reliability meets mission requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: Operating without defined SLAs can lead to misaligned expectations and difficulty in measuring service reliability.

choices.title: Service Level Objectives (SLOs) have not been defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice having defined SLOs. Continue maintaining clear SLO definitions as they provide concrete, measurable targets for service performance and reliability.

helpfulResource.displayText: Operating without defined SLOs makes it difficult to measure and improve service performance effectively.

choices.title: Unsure

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if you are uncertain about your workload's SLA/SLO definitions or status.

questions.title: Do your workload components scale dynamically in response to changes in demand?
questions.description: Review system diagram if available. Document manually scaled components in the notes field. Automated scaling is essential to maintain a responsive, resilient, and efficiently-managed cloud infrastructure.

choices.title: All components support dynamic scaling

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement dynamic scaling for all components to improve workload resilience, optimize resource utilization, and ensure automated response to demand changes. This is crucial for mission-critical workloads.

helpfulResource.displayText: Dynamic scaling automatically adjusts resources based on demand, improving both cost efficiency and performance during varying load conditions.

choices.title: Some components support dynamic scaling, others are manually scaled

improvementPlan.displayText: While mixed scaling approaches might be necessary in some cases, strive to implement dynamic scaling for all components where possible to maximize workload resilience and operational efficiency.

helpfulResource.displayText: Mixed scaling approaches may be appropriate when certain components have specific requirements or constraints that prevent automatic scaling.

choices.title: All components are manually scaled

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement dynamic scaling for appropriate components to improve responsiveness to demand changes and optimize resource utilization.

helpfulResource.displayText: Manual scaling increases operational overhead and may result in over-provisioning or performance issues during demand changes.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above scaling patterns match your workload's configuration.

questions.title: Are you planning for redundant network connectivity between AWS and on-premises environments?
questions.description: Highly-available connectivity is key to mission resilience. Review system diagram, if available.

choices.title: The workload leverages multiple (redundant) AWS Direct Connect connections, distributed to multiple locations

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement multiple AWS Direct Connect connections across different locations to achieve the highest level of network resilience. This configuration provides protection against both connection and location failures.

helpfulResource.displayText: Multiple AWS Direct Connect connections across different locations provide the highest level of network resilience for hybrid architectures.

choices.title: The workload leverages multiple (redundant) AWS Direct Connect connections to a single location

improvementPlan.displayText: If multi-location AWS Direct Connect isn't possible, implement multiple AWS Direct Connect connections at a single location as a minimum to protect against connection failures.

helpfulResource.displayText: Multiple connections to a single location protect against connection failures but remain vulnerable to location-specific outages.

choices.title: The workload leverages a single AWS Direct Connect connection

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice avoiding single AWS Direct Connect dependency. Continue to maintain redundant connections as single connections represent a significant risk to mission continuity.

helpfulResource.displayText: A single AWS Direct Connect connection represents a single point of failure for hybrid connectivity.

choices.title: The workload leverages redundant connections of another type. (describe in Notes Section)

improvementPlan.displayText: While redundant connections of other types provide some resilience, consider implementing AWS Direct Connect for improved reliability and lower latency. Regularly test failover procedures for your current solution.

helpfulResource.displayText: Alternative connectivity solutions with redundancy can provide high availability when properly implemented and maintained. Examples include virtual private networks (VPN) and software defined wide area networks (SD-WAN).

choices.title: The workload leverages a single connection of another type. (describe in Notes Section)

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice avoiding single connection dependency. Continue to maintain redundant connectivity to prevent single points of failure in your network architecture.

helpfulResource.displayText: Single connection architectures of any type represent a significant risk to mission continuity. Examples include virtual private networks (VPN) and software defined wide area networks (SD-WAN).

questions.title: What is the network path between your workload and other workloads running in AWS?
questions.description: When connecting multiple cloud workloads, some communication methods offer greater inherent resilience than others. Native cloud networking features like VPC Peering and Transit Gateway provide built-in redundancy and high availability. Review and discuss architecture diagram, if available.

choices.title: Network path established using AWS Transit Gateway with appropriate route tables and security controls

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider using Transit Gateway for connectivity. Review Transit Gateway route tables and security controls regularly to ensure they align with security requirements and resilience objectives.

helpfulResource.displayText: Transit Gateway provides a hub-and-spoke architecture with built-in redundancy and simplified management for complex networking requirements.

choices.title: Network path established using AWS PrivateLink (endpoint service)

improvementPlan.displayText: Utilize PrivateLink endpoints when possible. Ensure endpoint services are properly configured with redundant endpoints across availability zones.

helpfulResource.displayText: PrivateLink provides secure, private connectivity without exposing traffic to the public internet while maintaining high availability.

choices.title: Network path established using VPC Peering

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider Transit Gateway for complex networking requirements or when managing multiple VPC connections becomes challenging.

helpfulResource.displayText: VPC Peering provides direct network connectivity between VPCs with built-in redundancy, suitable for simple architectures.

choices.title: Network path leverages Transit VPC

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider migrating to AWS Transit Gateway for improved manageability, scalability, and built-in redundancy.

helpfulResource.displayText: Transit VPC architecture requires careful management of redundancy and failover mechanisms.

choices.title: Network path leverages on-premises network connectivity for VPC-to-VPC communication (hair-pinning)

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement direct AWS networking solutions (Transit Gateway, VPC Peering, or PrivateLink) to eliminate unnecessary network hops and reduce latency.

helpfulResource.displayText: Hair-pinning through on-premises networks introduces additional points of failure and increased latency.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the listed networking patterns match your workload's configuration.

questions.title: How does DNS (Domain Name System) complement your resilience strategy?
questions.description: DNS enables resilience by supporting health checks and automated failover. Within government networks, a service provider may be managing DNS on your behalf. Explore their capabilities to understand if DNS-based health checks are included. Consider how this affects your resilience strategy.

choices.title: Review and set appropriate TTL (Time to Live) values for resources

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate and configure DNS TTL values based on your workload's requirements for change propagation speed versus reliability and cost.

helpfulResource.displayText: TTL values (60-172,800 seconds) balance responsiveness and reliability. Shorter TTLs enable faster changes but increase query volume, while longer TTLs improve reliability and reduce costs through caching.

choices.title: Create DNS-based health checks for resources

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement health checks for critical resources to enable automated DNS-based failover capabilities.

helpfulResource.displayText: DNS health checks monitor resource availability and can trigger automated failover when issues are detected.

choices.title: Regular testing of health checks and DNS-based resource failover

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish and execute regular testing procedures for DNS failover mechanisms to ensure they function as expected.

helpfulResource.displayText: Regular testing validates failover configurations and ensures teams are familiar with DNS-based recovery procedures.

choices.title: Implement service discovery patterns using DNS (e.g., SRV records)

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement DNS-based service discovery to support dynamic scaling and automated failover of microservices.

helpfulResource.displayText: Service discovery supports dynamic scaling and failover of microservices, improving overall system resilience.

choices.title: Periodically review and clean up DNS records

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish regular DNS record maintenance procedures to remove outdated entries and validate existing configurations.

helpfulResource.displayText: Regular DNS maintenance ensures accurate records and removes potential points of failure from obsolete configurations.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the listed DNS resilience patterns are implemented in your workload.

questions.title: How does your workload access AWS service endpoints?
questions.description: Any AWS service that your workload depends on should be accessed via highly-available means. To connect programmatically to an AWS service, you use an endpoint. An endpoint is the URL (Uniform Resource Locator) of the entry point for an AWS web service.

choices.title: AWS service endpoints are accessed using VPC endpoints

improvementPlan.displayText: Review and adopt all available VPC endpoints for AWS services that your workload depends on.

helpfulResource.displayText: You can create an interface VPC endpoint to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink, including many AWS services. Gateway VPC endpoints provide reliable connectivity to Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB without requiring an internet gateway or a NAT device for your VPC. Gateway endpoints do not use AWS PrivateLink, unlike other types of VPC endpoints. Contact your AWS account team for information about endpoint support in ADC regions.

choices.title: AWS service endpoints are accessed using an Internet Gateway or (NAT Gateway + Internet Gateway)

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider implementing VPC endpoints where available to reduce dependency on internet connectivity.

helpfulResource.displayText: Internet and NAT gateways are horizontally scaled and highly available VPC components, but introduce internet dependency for AWS service access.

choices.title: Some AWS services are accessed via VPC endpoints, while others are accessed using public endpoints

improvementPlan.displayText: Review services using public endpoints and evaluate migration to VPC endpoints where available.

helpfulResource.displayText: Mixed endpoint access patterns may be necessary but should be regularly reviewed as new VPC endpoint capabilities become available.

choices.title: AWS service endpoints are accessed using a customer-managed proxy service with an acceptable level of support

improvementPlan.displayText: Document proxy service support requirements and regularly validate service levels are being met.

helpfulResource.displayText: (for example, 24/7/365 support) Customer-managed proxy services with robust support can provide additional control but require careful management of the proxy infrastructure.

choices.title: AWS service endpoints are accessed using a customer-managed proxy service with an unknown or unacceptable level of support

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish clear support requirements for proxy services or migrate to native AWS networking solutions.

helpfulResource.displayText: Proxy services without adequate support levels represent a significant risk to workload availability.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the listed endpoint access patterns match your workload's configuration.

questions.title: How have you planned for potential outages or degradation of cloud ingress points managed by a third-party?
questions.description: Highly regulated cloud workloads often rely on one and sometimes multiple cloud ingress points (e.g., BCAP (Boundary Cloud Access Point), ICAP (Internal Cloud Access Point), IAP Internet Access Point), CNAP (Cloud Native Access Point)). It is important to consider these as dependencies and plan for a 3rd party outage and how it might affect your mission.

choices.title: Workload uses multiple paths of ingress to avoid single point of failure or allow acceptable level of workload availability

improvementPlan.displayText: Identify an additional ingress path to increase workload availability.

helpfulResource.displayText: Multiple ingress paths enhance resilience against third-party outages or degradation.

choices.title: Workload uses single ingress point.

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate and implement additional ingress paths to mitigate single point of failure risks.

helpfulResource.displayText: Single ingress points introduce significant risk of major workload degradation during outages.

choices.title: Mission is aware of ingress point(s) SLA(s)

improvementPlan.displayText: Review SLAs regularly and ensure they align with mission requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: Understanding ingress point SLAs is crucial for effective mission planning and risk assessment.

choices.title: Mission is not aware of current ingress point(s), ingress SLAs, or current level of risk

improvementPlan.displayText: Identify and document all ingress points, their SLAs, and associated risks to the mission.

helpfulResource.displayText: Lack of awareness about ingress points and their SLAs can lead to unexpected mission impacts.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above options accurately describe your ingress planning.

questions.title: Are you planning for network resilience for edge environments?
questions.description: An edge computing environment brings compute, storage, and networking resources closer to where data is generated, including environments such as AWS Modular Data Centers. For mission-critical edge deployments, network resilience is essential for maintaining operational capabilities in contested or degraded environments. Different network types and redundant connections help ensure continued operations during disruptions. These environments are often deployed in austere conditions, and may be susceptible to events that impact network resilience. Carefully consider network resilience when deploying resources to the edge.

choices.title: Edge environments are connected using multiple network connections of different types.

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement diverse network connectivity types (such as combining terrestrial and satellite communications) to achieve maximum resilience against different types of failures. This provides the highest level of protection against network disruptions in edge environments.

helpfulResource.displayText: Diverse network types (terrestrial and SATCOM) provide the highest level of resilience against different failure modes and environmental challenges.

choices.title: Edge environments are connected using multiple network connections of the same type

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider implementing diverse network types (such as combining terrestrial and SATCOM) to protect against type-specific failures. While multiple connections of the same type provide some redundancy, diverse network types offer superior resilience.

helpfulResource.displayText: Multiple connections of the same type provide redundancy but may be vulnerable to type-specific disruptions.

choices.title: Edge environments are connected using a single network connection

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice avoiding single network connections for edge environments. Continue to maintain multiple, diverse network connections to ensure resilience against network disruptions and environmental events. Consider implementing both terrestrial and satellite communications for maximum protection.

helpfulResource.displayText: Single network connections represent a significant risk to edge operations during network disruptions or environmental events.

questions.title: For edge workloads, have you tested the workload behavior with disconnected, intermittent, and/or limited network conditions?
questions.description: For architectures leveraging both cloud and edge components, a robust Concept of Employment (CONEMP) is crucial for ensuring mission success across all operational phases and potential failure scenarios. This question assesses whether the CONEMP adequately addresses the full lifecycle of applications, including AWS cloud-based components, edge deployments, and hybrid architectures, while accounting for various failure modes and degraded operational conditions.

choices.title: The operating conditions of Denied, Degraded, Intermittent and Limited (DDIL) tolerances are clearly defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Research and understand each DDIL scenario your workload is required to operate within.

helpfulResource.displayText: Clearly defined DDIL tolerances are essential for effective edge workload planning and testing.

choices.title: Each of the major components have been tested when communications are disrupted

improvementPlan.displayText: Create a plan to test each component within a disrupted communications DDIL scenario.

helpfulResource.displayText: Testing under disrupted communications helps ensure workload resilience in challenging environments.

choices.title: Each of the major components have been tested when communications are intermittent or unreliable

improvementPlan.displayText: Create a plan to test each component within an intermittent communications DDIL scenario.

helpfulResource.displayText: Intermittent communication testing validates workload behavior under realistic edge conditions.

choices.title: Each of the major components have been tested under low bandwidth and/or high latency conditions

improvementPlan.displayText: Create a plan to test each component within a high-latency communications DDIL scenario.

helpfulResource.displayText: Low bandwidth and high latency testing ensures workload functionality in constrained network environments.

choices.title: AWS service control plane dependencies have been reviewed and are understood

improvementPlan.displayText: Review each AWS service that your workload depends on, and understand the impact of a control plane outage within DDIL scenarios.

helpfulResource.displayText: Understanding control plane dependencies is crucial for managing edge workload behavior during service disruptions.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above DDIL testing scenarios have been implemented for your edge workload.

questions.title: How do you manage your Amazon VPC CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) ranges to accommodate substantial scaling events?
questions.description: Subnet capacity constraints can impact scaling in the event of a mission event. Managed services such as Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS), Elastic Load Balancing (ELB), and AWS Lambda will consume additional VPC IP addresses during scale-out events. For example, a single Application Load Balancer can consume up to 8 IP addresses per AZ, each EKS node requires an IP address, PrivateLink endpoints consume an IP per AZ, and NAT Gateways each require a dedicated IP.

choices.title: VPC subnets have ample capacity to support scaling events

improvementPlan.displayText: Review IP consumption patterns of managed services: EKS nodes (1 IP per node), Application Load Balancer (ALB) (8 IPs per AZ), NAT Gateways (1 IP each), and AWS PrivateLink endpoints (1 IP per AZ). Calculate projected IP needs based on maximum scaling scenarios.

helpfulResource.displayText: Ample subnet capacity ensures your workload can scale effectively during mission-critical events.

choices.title: VPC includes unused CIDR ranges to support significant scaling events

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly review unused CIDR ranges to ensure they remain available for future scaling needs. Consider implementing a CIDR management process to track and allocate ranges efficiently.

helpfulResource.displayText: Unused CIDR ranges provide flexibility for future expansion and unforeseen scaling requirements.

choices.title: Workload scaling is at-risk due to constrained CIDR block capacity

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate options to expand VPC CIDR ranges or implement more efficient IP address allocation strategies. Consider using larger CIDR blocks or implementing additional secondary CIDR blocks.

helpfulResource.displayText: Constrained CIDR capacity can limit workload scalability and resilience during critical events.

choices.title: We have not evaluated CIDR block capacity recently

improvementPlan.displayText: Conduct a thorough review of current CIDR block usage and project future needs based on expected scaling events. Implement a regular CIDR capacity review process.

helpfulResource.displayText: Regular evaluation of CIDR capacity is crucial for maintaining scalability and preventing unexpected constraints.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above options accurately describe your CIDR management approach.

questions.title: How do you reserve capacity for mission-critical workload functions?
questions.description: Several cloud services offer methods to reserve capacity. Capacity can be reserved through various mechanisms: Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances for steady-state workloads, On-Demand Capacity Reservations for immediate availability, and service-specific reservations like AWS Lambda Provisioned Concurrency for consistent performance.

choices.title: Amazon EC2: Reserved Instances (Zonal)

improvementPlan.displayText: Review your zonal Reserved Instance strategy to ensure it aligns with your mission-critical workload requirements and availability needs.

helpfulResource.displayText: Zonal Reserved Instances provide capacity reservations in a specific Availability Zone, offering both a capacity reservation and potential cost savings.

choices.title: Amazon EC2: On-demand Capacity Reservations

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate your On-Demand Capacity Reservation usage and adjust as needed to ensure immediate availability for mission-critical workloads.

helpfulResource.displayText: On-Demand Capacity Reservations allow you to reserve compute capacity for your Amazon EC2 instances in a specific Availability Zone for any duration.

choices.title: Capacity reservation (or provisioned throughput/concurrency) for another AWS service (list in the Notes Section)

improvementPlan.displayText: Review and optimize your capacity reservations for other AWS services to ensure they meet your mission-critical workload requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: Many AWS services offer capacity reservation options, such as Amazon DynamoDB reserved capacity or AWS Lambda provisioned concurrency, to ensure consistent performance for critical workloads.

choices.title: No capacity reservations

improvementPlan.displayText: Assess your mission-critical workload requirements and consider implementing appropriate capacity reservations to ensure availability during peak demand.

helpfulResource.displayText: Operating without capacity reservations may expose mission-critical workloads to potential resource unavailability during high-demand periods.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above options accurately describe your capacity reservation strategy.

questions.title: How does your workload react to unexpected increases in request volume?
questions.description: Unexpected increases in request volume can lead to resource exhaustion, degraded performance, or system failures. Understanding and implementing appropriate controls like throttling, caching, and backoff strategies is crucial for maintaining workload reliability.

choices.title: Automatic request throttling

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement automatic request throttling to mitigate resource exhaustion. Requests below throttling rates should be processed while those over the defined limit should return a throttling message.

helpfulResource.displayText: Request throttling helps protect your workload by rejecting excess requests when demand exceeds defined thresholds.

choices.title: Emergency Levers/Circuit breakers

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement circuit breakers to prevent cascade failures and allow graceful degradation during periods of excessive load.

helpfulResource.displayText: Circuit breakers help maintain system stability by temporarily disabling problematic components during overload conditions.

choices.title: Cached responses

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement caching strategies to reduce load on backend services and improve response times during high-volume periods.

helpfulResource.displayText: Caching can significantly reduce backend load and improve response times during periods of high request volume.

choices.title: Timeouts

improvementPlan.displayText: Set appropriate timeouts on connections and requests, verify them systematically, and avoid relying on default values.

helpfulResource.displayText: Well-configured timeouts prevent resource exhaustion by limiting the duration of requests and connections.

choices.title: Exponential backoff

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement exponential backoff with jitter for retries to prevent thundering herd problems during recovery.

helpfulResource.displayText: Exponential backoff with jitter helps distribute retry attempts and prevent system overload during recovery.

choices.title: Rate-limiting

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement rate-limiting controls to maintain consistent performance and prevent resource exhaustion.

helpfulResource.displayText: Rate-limiting helps maintain system stability by controlling the flow of requests to match processing capacity.

choices.title: No throttles or rate-limits on requests

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement request controls to prevent resource exhaustion. Consider throttling, rate-limiting, and failing fast when services are overwhelmed.

helpfulResource.displayText: Operating without request controls exposes your workload to risks from unexpected volume increases.

questions.title: Are Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) defined for your workload? If so, how are they instrumented?
questions.description: Key performance indicators (KPIs) are quantifiable measurements that help you understand how well you're performing in specific areas. KPIs might include system availability, response time, error rates, and mission-specific metrics that directly relate to operational effectiveness. KPIs can be used to trigger remediation automatically, or inform workload operators to execute a runbook.

choices.title: KPIs are defined, and instrumented via dashboards and/or alarms

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement comprehensive KPI instrumentation using dashboards and alarms to gain real-time visibility into workload performance and enable automated responses to conditions.

helpfulResource.displayText: Well-instrumented KPIs provide real-time visibility into workload performance and mission readiness.

choices.title: KPIs are aligned with and traceable to specific mission objectives

improvementPlan.displayText: Align your KPIs with specific mission objectives to ensure measurements directly reflect operational effectiveness and mission success criteria.

helpfulResource.displayText: Mission-aligned KPIs ensure that technical measurements translate directly to operational effectiveness.

choices.title: KPIs are defined, but not instrumented

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice having defined KPIs. Continue by implementing instrumentation using CloudWatch metrics, dashboards, and alarms to enable real-time visibility and automated responses.

helpfulResource.displayText: Defined KPIs require instrumentation to provide actionable insights and enable automated responses.

choices.title: KPIs are not defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice acknowledging the need for KPIs. Begin by defining KPIs that align with your mission objectives, then implement appropriate monitoring and instrumentation.

helpfulResource.displayText: Without defined KPIs, it's difficult to measure workload performance and mission readiness effectively.

questions.title: How do you monitor workload resources?
questions.description: Logs and metrics are powerful tools to gain insight into the health of your workload. You can configure your workload to monitor logs and metrics and send notifications when thresholds are crossed or significant events occur. Monitoring enables your workload to recognize when low-performance thresholds are crossed or failures occur, so it can recover automatically in response. (Aligns with AWS Well Architected Framework question Reliability #6)

choices.title: Monitor all components for the workload (Generation)

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement comprehensive monitoring across all workload components, including custom metrics for mission-specific requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: Comprehensive component monitoring provides the foundation for understanding workload health and performance.

choices.title: Define and calculate metrics (Aggregation)

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish clear metric definitions and implement aggregation to provide meaningful insights into workload performance.

helpfulResource.displayText: Well-defined metrics enable effective decision-making and automated responses to conditions.

choices.title: Send notifications and automate responses (Real-time processing and alarming)

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement automated notifications and responses based on defined thresholds and conditions.

helpfulResource.displayText: Automated responses help maintain workload health by taking immediate action when issues are detected.

choices.title: Analyze logs and conduct regular reviews

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement log analysis practices and establish regular review procedures to identify trends and potential issues.

helpfulResource.displayText: Log analysis provides deep insights into workload behavior and helps identify potential issues before they impact operations.

choices.title: Monitor end-to-end tracing of requests through your system

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement distributed tracing to understand request flows and dependencies across your workload.

helpfulResource.displayText: End-to-end tracing helps understand request paths and identify bottlenecks in distributed systems.

questions.title: Have Amazon EC2-based mission components been performance-tested to run on multiple instance types or sizes?
questions.description: Performance testing across instance types not only helps mitigate capacity shortages but can also optimize cost-performance ratios and improve mission resilience during regional capacity constraints. Leveraging different instance types or sizes can mitigate the impact of capacity shortages. Amazon EC2 features such as mixed-type autoscaling groups can automate this strategy.

choices.title: Core components have been performance-tested, and can run on multiple instance types or sizes

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly review and update instance type compatibility testing to ensure optimal performance across supported configurations.

helpfulResource.displayText: Supporting multiple instance types increases resilience against capacity constraints and enables cost optimization.

choices.title: Core components have been performance-tested, and are limited to one instance type and size

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate and test component compatibility with alternative instance types to improve resilience against capacity constraints.

helpfulResource.displayText: Single instance type dependencies can create risks during capacity constraints or regional limitations.

choices.title: Core components have not been performance-tested to run on different instance types or sizes

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and implement a performance testing strategy that includes evaluation across multiple instance types and sizes.

helpfulResource.displayText: Lack of performance testing across instance types limits understanding of workload behavior and scaling options.

questions.title: Does your workload utilize distributed tracing?
questions.description: Distributed tracing frameworks emit transactions and state information throughout the lifecycle of requests. Distributed tracing helps identify mission-critical dependencies, latency issues, and failure points by providing end-to-end visibility of request flows across system components. By capturing trace data from multiple sources and analyzing it in a unified view, teams can better understand how requests flow, where bottlenecks exist, and where optimization efforts should focus. Examples of tracing tools include: Zipkin, Jaeger, & AWS X-Ray.

choices.title: Distributed tracing tools are integrated into the workload

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly review and optimize your distributed tracing implementation to ensure comprehensive coverage and actionable insights.

helpfulResource.displayText: Integrated distributed tracing provides invaluable insights into system behavior and performance.

choices.title: Distributed tracing tools are not used in the workload

improvementPlan.displayText: Evaluate and implement a distributed tracing solution to gain visibility into request flows and system dependencies.

helpfulResource.displayText: Lack of distributed tracing can hinder troubleshooting and performance optimization in complex systems.

choices.title: Workload is not a distributed system (the workload is monolithic and does not utilize a microservices design pattern)

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider implementing basic tracing or logging to gain insights into request flows within your monolithic application.

helpfulResource.displayText: Even monolithic applications can benefit from tracing to understand internal request flows and performance bottlenecks.

questions.title: How do you design your workload to withstand component failures?
questions.description: For highly regulated workloads, comprehensive component failure testing is essential as it validates the workload's resilience against both anticipated and unexpected failures that could impact operations. Component failures in mission-critical systems could include network connectivity loss, compute resource exhaustion, or data storage failures, each requiring specific resilience strategies aligned with cybersecurity requirements. Regular testing with clear responsibilities and notification procedures ensures rapid response to actual failures and maintains operational readiness. (Aligns with AWS Well Architected Framework question Reliability #11)

choices.title: Monitor all components for the workload to detect failures

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement comprehensive health checks and monitoring across all workload components with appropriate thresholds and alerting.

helpfulResource.displayText: Effective monitoring enables early detection of potential failures and supports proactive resolution.

choices.title: Fail over to healthy resources and automate healing on all layers

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement automated failover mechanisms and self-healing capabilities across all workload components.

helpfulResource.displayText: Automated healing and failover capabilities minimize downtime and maintain mission readiness.

choices.title: Use static stability to prevent bimodal behavior and rely on the data plane during recovery

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement static stability patterns and ensure recovery procedures prioritize data plane operations.

helpfulResource.displayText: Static stability ensures predictable behavior during failures and recovery operations.

choices.title: Send notifications when events impact availability and breach SLA targets

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement robust notification systems and design architecture to meet availability requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: Effective notification systems ensure rapid response to availability impacts and SLA breaches.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above failure resilience mechanisms are implemented in your workload.

questions.title: During a widespread outage affecting multiple systems, how does your service behave if it recovers before its dependencies?
questions.description: In military and intelligence operations, workloads must continue functioning even when facing partial failures or degraded conditions. Graceful degradation ensures that critical capabilities remain operational, even if at reduced capacity. Maintaining some level of operational capability, even in degraded conditions, can provide a strategic advantage over adversaries who might experience complete system failures.

choices.title: Workload performs health checks against services it depends on

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement comprehensive health checks for all dependencies, including timeout configurations and fallback behaviors.

helpfulResource.displayText: Health checks provide visibility into dependency status and enable intelligent recovery decisions.

choices.title: Workload has been tested against a scenario where services it depends on are not available during steady-state operation

improvementPlan.displayText: Conduct regular testing of dependency failure scenarios during normal operations, including partial and complete dependency outages.

helpfulResource.displayText: Testing steady-state dependency failures helps ensure graceful degradation capabilities.

choices.title: Workload start-up has been tested against a scenario where services it depends on are not available

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement and test start-up procedures that account for dependency unavailability, including proper ordering and fallback mechanisms.

helpfulResource.displayText: Start-up testing with unavailable dependencies ensures recovery capability in various degraded states.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above dependency recovery mechanisms are implemented in your workload.

questions.title: Have you reviewed the availability SLAs of your workload's external dependencies?
questions.description: Examples of external dependencies include services like Helper VPCs, proxy servers, Virtual Data Center Managed Services (VDMS & VDSS), & Internet Access Points (IAP), AWS services, enterprise-provided NTP, DNS, SFTP, etc. Understanding dependency SLAs is crucial for assessing overall mission readiness and designing appropriate resilience strategies to meet operational requirements.

choices.title: Availability SLAs for dependencies have been reviewed, goals/SLAs are acceptable

improvementPlan.displayText: Review and document SLAs for all dependencies, ensuring they meet your mission requirements. Implement regular SLA review processes to maintain mission readiness.

helpfulResource.displayText: Acceptable SLAs provide a foundation for reliable mission operations, but continuous monitoring is essential.

choices.title: Availability SLAs for dependencies have been reviewed, goals/SLAs are insufficient or unavailable

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice reviewing SLAs. Continue by identifying alternative solutions or implementing additional resilience measures to address gaps in dependency SLAs.

helpfulResource.displayText: Insufficient SLAs may require architectural changes or additional redundancy to meet mission requirements.

choices.title: Availability SLAs for dependencies have not been reviewed

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice acknowledging the need for SLA review. Begin by conducting a comprehensive review of all dependency SLAs and assess their impact on overall workload availability.

helpfulResource.displayText: Unreviewed SLAs represent unknown risks to mission readiness and operational capabilities.

questions.title: Does your operations team have visibility into the health of your workload's external dependencies?
questions.description: Dependency telemetry is essential for monitoring the health and performance of the external services and components your workload relies on. Examples include: reachability or response time of resources the system depends on, such as: external databases, data feeds, DNS, and network connectivity. An example implementation is a metrics dashboard provided to your workload operators. For highly regulated workloads, real-time visibility into dependency health is crucial for maintaining operational readiness and responding rapidly to potential issues that could impact mission success.

choices.title: Operations Team has visibility into the health of external services the workload depends on

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly review and enhance monitoring capabilities to ensure comprehensive visibility into all critical dependencies.

helpfulResource.displayText: Comprehensive dependency monitoring enables proactive issue detection and rapid response to potential service disruptions.

choices.title: Operations Team has no visibility into the health of external services the workload depends on

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement monitoring and dashboards to provide visibility into the health and performance of external dependencies.

helpfulResource.displayText: Lack of dependency monitoring can lead to delayed issue detection and extended service disruptions.

choices.title: Unsure

helpfulResource.displayText: Uncertainty about monitoring capabilities indicates a need to review and document dependency oversight.

questions.title: How does your workload handle Cross Domain System dependencies and potential outages?
questions.description: A CDS is an integrated software-hardware system that makes secure access to and exchange of sensitive data possible across networks between various levels of security classification, including incompatible security domains. In military and intelligence environments, CDS dependencies are often mission-critical, and understanding their SLAs and outage behaviors is essential for maintaining operational continuity across security domains.

choices.title: This workload has a CDS dependency with a documented SLA

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly review the CDS SLA to ensure it continues to meet mission requirements and update contingency plans as needed.

helpfulResource.displayText: A documented SLA provides a clear understanding of CDS performance expectations and supports effective contingency planning.

choices.title: This workload has a CDS dependency with an unknown or undocumented SLA

improvementPlan.displayText: Engage with the CDS operator to obtain or establish a documented SLA, and develop contingency plans based on potential service levels.

helpfulResource.displayText: Lack of a documented SLA introduces uncertainty in operational planning and may impact mission readiness.

choices.title: During a CDS outage, a component queues CDS transfer requests

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly test and optimize the queuing mechanism to ensure it can handle extended CDS outages without impacting critical operations.

helpfulResource.displayText: Queuing CDS requests during outages helps maintain data integrity and supports eventual consistency across domains.

choices.title: During a CDS outage, the workload does not queue CDS transfer requests

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement a queuing mechanism for CDS requests during outages to prevent data loss and ensure eventual consistency.

helpfulResource.displayText: Lack of request queuing during CDS outages may lead to data loss or inconsistency across security domains.

questions.title: What is your strategy for managing certificate expiration?
questions.description: Digital certificates are critical security components that require deliberate management to prevent unexpected expiration and potential service disruptions. In mission-critical systems, certificate expiration can lead to immediate service outages and security compliance violations.

choices.title: Digital certificates are automatically renewed before expiration

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly review and test your automated renewal process to ensure it remains effective and covers all critical certificates.

helpfulResource.displayText: Automated renewal minimizes the risk of unexpected certificate expiration and reduces operational overhead.

choices.title: Certificates are manually renewed with alarms/notifications for impending expiration

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider implementing automated renewal for critical certificates while maintaining alerting as a backup mechanism.

helpfulResource.displayText: Alerting helps prevent unexpected expirations, but manual renewal still carries some risk and operational burden.

choices.title: Certificates are manually renewed following a documented procedure (runbook)

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement monitoring and alerting for certificate expiration, and consider automation for high-volume or critical certificates.

helpfulResource.displayText: Documented procedures ensure consistency but may not scale well for large numbers of certificates or prevent human error.

choices.title: Certificates are manually renewed without a formal procedure

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and document certificate renewal procedures, implement expiration monitoring, and consider automation options.

helpfulResource.displayText: Lack of formal procedures for certificate management increases the risk of unexpected expirations and security incidents.

questions.title: How does your workload behave when an Identity Provider (IdP)/OCSP/CRL endpoint is non-responsive?
questions.description: These components (Identity Providers, Online Certificate Status Protocol, and Certificate Revocation Lists) are crucial for secure operations, authenticating users, validating certificates in real-time, and maintaining records of invalid certificates. Failure of these services can significantly impact authentication and access control capabilities. For highly regulated customers concerned with IdP/OCSP/CRL availability, it's important to understand that certificate status endpoints are designed with inherent availability limitations.

choices.title: Multiple IDP and OCSP endpoints. CRL is cached to provide high availability

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly test and validate the failover mechanisms between multiple endpoints to ensure continued high availability.

helpfulResource.displayText: Multiple endpoints and CRL caching provide the highest level of resilience against IdP/OCSP/CRL failures.

choices.title: Regular testing proves alternate endpoints and CRL caches successfully provide authentication

improvementPlan.displayText: Consider implementing additional endpoints for increased redundancy and explore automated failover mechanisms.

helpfulResource.displayText: Regular testing ensures the reliability of alternate endpoints and CRL caches in authentication scenarios.

choices.title: Graceful degradation of functionality

improvementPlan.displayText: Document and regularly review graceful degradation procedures. Consider implementing additional redundancy measures.

helpfulResource.displayText: Graceful degradation allows for continued operation with reduced functionality during endpoint failures.

choices.title: Error is logged and alerts are generated

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement graceful degradation procedures and explore options for endpoint redundancy to improve resilience.

helpfulResource.displayText: Logging and alerting provide awareness of endpoint failures but do not inherently provide continued functionality.

choices.title: An operations dashboard displays alerts

improvementPlan.displayText: Enhance monitoring with automated alerts and develop procedures for graceful degradation during endpoint failures.

helpfulResource.displayText: Dashboard alerts provide visibility into endpoint status but require manual intervention during failures.

choices.title: Workload stops responding or issues critical error

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement error handling, logging, and alerting. Develop a strategy for graceful degradation during endpoint failures.

helpfulResource.displayText: Critical failures during endpoint unavailability represent a significant risk to operational continuity.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above options accurately describe your workload's behavior during IdP/OCSP/CRL endpoint failures.

questions.title: How do you design interactions in a distributed system to prevent failures?
questions.description: Distributed systems rely on communications networks to interconnect components, such as servers or services. In mission-critical environments, distributed system failures can cascade rapidly, potentially impacting operational capabilities. Your workload must operate reliably despite data loss or latency in these networks. Components of the distributed system must operate in a way that does not negatively impact other components or the workload. These best practices prevent failures and improve mean time between failures (MTBF) (Aligns with AWS Well Architected Framework question Reliability #4).

choices.title: Implement loosely coupled dependencies

improvementPlan.displayText: Enhance system resilience by implementing queuing systems, streaming systems, and load balancing to reduce direct dependencies.

helpfulResource.displayText: Loosely coupled architectures improve system resilience by reducing direct dependencies between components.

choices.title: Make all responses idempotent

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement idempotency tokens and design APIs to ensure multiple identical requests have the same effect as a single request.

helpfulResource.displayText: Idempotent operations ensure system consistency and reliability during retries and duplicate requests.

choices.title: Identify the kind of distributed systems you depend on

improvementPlan.displayText: Document system dependencies, communication patterns, and interaction models to better understand potential failure modes.

helpfulResource.displayText: Understanding your distributed system patterns is fundamental to preventing cascading failures.

choices.title: Do constant work

improvementPlan.displayText: Design systems for predictable resource utilization and avoid large, rapid changes in load.

helpfulResource.displayText: Consistent workload patterns help maintain system stability and prevent resource exhaustion.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above distributed system failure prevention methods are implemented.

questions.title: How do you use fault isolation to protect your workload?
questions.description: Fault isolated boundaries limit the effect of a failure within a workload to a limited number of components. Components outside of the boundary are unaffected by the failure. In mission-critical environments, fault isolation is essential to prevent cascading failures that could impact operational capabilities. Using multiple fault isolated boundaries helps contain failures and maintain critical functions even when components fail. (Aligns with AWS Well Architected Framework question Reliability #10)

choices.title: Deploy the workload to multiple locations

improvementPlan.displayText: Distribute workload data and resources across multiple Availability Zones or, where necessary, across AWS Regions.

helpfulResource.displayText: Distribute workload data and resources across multiple Availability Zones or, where necessary, across AWS Regions. These locations can be as diverse as required.

choices.title: Select the appropriate locations for your multi-location deployment

improvementPlan.displayText: Deploy workload components to multiple Availability Zones for high availability and evaluate options for multi-Region architecture for extreme resilience requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: For high availability, always (when possible) deploy your workload components to multiple Availability Zones (AZs). For workloads with extreme resilience requirements, carefully evaluate the options for a multi-Region architecture.

choices.title: Use bulkhead architectures to limit scope of impact

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement bulkhead architectures to restrict the effect of failure within a workload to a limited number of components.

helpfulResource.displayText: Implement bulkhead architectures (also known as cell-based architectures) to restrict the effect of failure within a workload to a limited number of components.

choices.title: Automate recovery for components constrained to a single location

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement the capability to do a complete rebuild of the workload within your defined recovery objectives.

helpfulResource.displayText: If components of the workload can only run in a single Availability Zone or in an on-premises data center, implement the capability to do a complete rebuild of the workload within your defined recovery objectives.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Choose this if your workload does not follow these fault isolation best practices.

questions.title: Have you constructed a failure model for the workload's components and dependencies?
questions.description: In mission-critical environments, a comprehensive failure model is essential for understanding potential points of failure, their impacts, and mitigation strategies. This proactive approach helps maintain operational readiness and minimizes downtime during critical missions. Your failure model should include columns for Component or Dependency, Failure Type, Service Impact, and Customer Impact.

choices.title: Failure model documented

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly review and update your failure model to reflect changes in components, dependencies, and mission requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: A comprehensive failure model provides the foundation for understanding and mitigating potential system failures.

choices.title: Soft failures known and documented

improvementPlan.displayText: Document all identified soft failures and their potential impacts on mission operations.

helpfulResource.displayText: Understanding and documenting soft failures helps prevent service degradation and maintain operational capabilities.

choices.title: Soft failures conditions are actively monitored for occurrence

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement comprehensive monitoring for all identified soft failure conditions and ensure appropriate alerting mechanisms.

helpfulResource.displayText: Active monitoring of soft failure conditions enables early detection and proactive mitigation.

choices.title: Known soft failure conditions have documented mitigations or playbooks

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly test and update mitigation playbooks for soft failure conditions to ensure their effectiveness.

helpfulResource.displayText: Documented mitigation strategies ensure consistent and effective response to soft failures.

choices.title: Hard failures known and documented

improvementPlan.displayText: Document all identified hard failures and their potential impacts on mission operations.

helpfulResource.displayText: Understanding and documenting hard failures is crucial for developing effective recovery strategies.

choices.title: Known hard failure conditions are actively monitored for occurrence

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement comprehensive monitoring for all identified hard failure conditions with appropriate alerting thresholds.

helpfulResource.displayText: Active monitoring of hard failure conditions enables rapid detection and response.

choices.title: Known hard failure conditions have documented mitigations or playbooks

improvementPlan.displayText: Regularly test and update mitigation playbooks for hard failure conditions to ensure their effectiveness.

helpfulResource.displayText: Documented mitigation strategies ensure consistent and effective response to hard failures.

choices.title: None of these

helpfulResource.displayText: Select this if none of the above failure modeling practices are implemented.

questions.title: Have Recovery Time Objective (RTO) and Recovery Point Objective (RPO) been defined for your workload?
questions.description: Recovery Time Objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable delay between the interruption of service and restoration of service. This determines what is considered an acceptable time window when service is unavailable. Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last data recovery point. This determines what is considered an acceptable loss of data between the last recovery point and the interruption of service. In highly regulated contexts, precisely defined RTO and RPO are crucial for maintaining operational readiness and ensuring mission continuity during service interruptions or data loss events. Both RTO and RPO are driven by the organization's mission requirements and inform the design of the technical architecture.

choices.title: Recovery Time Objective is defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Define clear RTO objectives based on mission requirements and implement technical controls to ensure these objectives can be met consistently.

helpfulResource.displayText: A well-defined RTO ensures clear expectations for service restoration timeframes.

choices.title: Recovery Point Objective is defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Define clear RPO objectives based on mission requirements and implement appropriate data protection controls to meet these objectives.

helpfulResource.displayText: A well-defined RPO ensures clear expectations for acceptable data loss during recovery.

choices.title: Recovery Time Objective is not defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice acknowledging the need for RTO definition. Define RTO based on mission requirements and implement appropriate technical controls to meet service restoration objectives.

helpfulResource.displayText: Undefined RTO can lead to misaligned recovery strategies and extended service disruptions.

choices.title: Recovery Point Objective is not defined

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice acknowledging the need for RPO definition. Define RPO based on mission requirements and implement appropriate data protection controls to prevent unexpected data loss.

helpfulResource.displayText: Undefined RPO can lead to unexpected data loss during recovery events.

questions.title: What is your strategy for disaster recovery? Is data replicated as part of your strategy?
questions.description: Disaster Recovery strategies involve cost and complexity tradeoffs. In mission-critical environments, a well-defined disaster recovery strategy is essential for maintaining operational capabilities during significant disruptions. The chosen strategy must balance recovery speed, cost, and complexity while ensuring mission continuity. Consider your specific RTO/RPO requirements when selecting a strategy.

choices.title: Active/Active

improvementPlan.displayText: While Active/Active provides the highest availability, it's also the most complex and costly. Regularly assess if this strategy aligns with your mission's RTO/RPO requirements and budget constraints. Consider less complex options if they can meet your recovery objectives.

helpfulResource.displayText: Active/Active provides continuous operation across multiple regions with real-time data replication, but at a higher cost and complexity.

choices.title: Warm Standby

improvementPlan.displayText: Warm Standby offers a good balance of recovery speed and cost. If your RTO/RPO requirements are more stringent, consider moving towards an Active/Active strategy. If they're less stringent, evaluate if a Pilot Light approach could meet your needs at a lower cost.

helpfulResource.displayText: Warm Standby maintains a scaled-down but ready-to-scale-up version of the production environment, balancing cost and recovery time.

choices.title: Pilot Light

improvementPlan.displayText: Pilot Light is cost-effective but may have longer recovery times. Assess if this strategy meets your RTO/RPO requirements. If faster recovery is needed, consider upgrading to Warm Standby. For less critical workloads, evaluate if Backup & Restore could suffice.

helpfulResource.displayText: Pilot Light keeps core systems running minimally, ready to scale up when needed, offering a balance between cost and recovery time.

choices.title: Backup & Restore

improvementPlan.displayText: While cost-effective, Backup & Restore typically has the longest recovery times. Evaluate if this aligns with your RTO/RPO requirements. For critical workloads or those with stricter recovery objectives, consider more robust strategies like Pilot Light or Warm Standby.

helpfulResource.displayText: Backup & Restore provides basic recovery capabilities at the lowest cost but with longer recovery times.

choices.title: Data is replicated as part of strategy

improvementPlan.displayText: Data replication is crucial for minimizing data loss. Ensure your replication strategy aligns with your RPO. For critical data with near-zero RPO, consider continuous replication methods, balancing the increased cost with your recovery requirements.

helpfulResource.displayText: Data replication is essential for minimizing data loss, but consider the cost-benefit ratio based on your specific RPO requirements.

choices.title: Data is not replicated as part of strategy

improvementPlan.displayText: Good practice recognizing the need for data replication. Implement data replication aligned with your RPO requirements. Start with critical data and gradually expand based on recovery needs and budget constraints.

helpfulResource.displayText: Lack of data replication can lead to significant data loss and extended recovery times. Evaluate the cost of potential data loss against the cost of replication.

questions.title: If employing a Backup & Restore DR/COOP strategy, are the following in place?
questions.description: The Backup & Restore DR/COOP strategy is a cost effective approach for many workloads. In mission environments, even a basic Backup & Restore DR/COOP strategy requires careful preparation and regular validation to ensure successful recovery to the DR site when needed. While this approach may be cost-effective, its success depends on having all essential components ready and tested. Besides regular data replication, there are still essential elements that must be in the target environment for a complete DR/COOP strategy.

choices.title: Data replicated and ready to go

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement automated data replication with regular validation checks to ensure data consistency and availability.

helpfulResource.displayText: Regular data replication is the foundation of a successful Backup & Restore strategy.

choices.title: Infrastructure as code to support creation of mission DR/COOP environment

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and maintain Infrastructure as Code templates for automated DR environment deployment.

helpfulResource.displayText: Infrastructure as Code ensures consistent and repeatable DR environment creation.

choices.title: Configuration management tools

improvementPlan.displayText: Implement and maintain configuration management tools to ensure consistent DR environment setup.

helpfulResource.displayText: Configuration management tools help manage configuration drift between production and DR environments.

choices.title: Certificate solution in-place in the DR/COOP site

improvementPlan.displayText: Establish processes for certificate management and renewal in the DR environment.

helpfulResource.displayText: Proper certificate management is crucial for secure DR operations.

choices.title: Configuration Standard Operating Procedure/Runbook

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and maintain detailed configuration procedures for DR environment setup.

helpfulResource.displayText: Well-documented configuration procedures ensure consistent DR environment setup.

choices.title: Cutover Standard Operating Procedure/Runbook

improvementPlan.displayText: Develop and regularly test cutover procedures to ensure smooth transition to DR environment.

helpfulResource.displayText: Clear cutover procedures are essential for successful DR activation.
